1. Core Clinical Tension: A 45-year-old Guatemalan immigrant with alcoholic cirrhosis and ESRD on hemodialysis presents with progressive abdominal distension and massive, exudative, hemorrhagic pleural effusions with marked fluid and peripheral eosinophilia. The clinical presentation mimics malignant peritoneal/pleural carcinomatosis, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, or hypereosinophilic syndrome, obscuring an invasive soil-transmitted helminthic hyperinfection.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The breakpoint occurs following initial emergency evaluation, cross-sectional CT/ultrasound imaging, and initial diagnostic thoracentesis confirming an exudative eosinophil-predominant pleural effusion, prior to bone marrow biopsy, flow cytometry, autoimmune panels, and send-out helminth serology.
3. Differential Distinctions: Peritoneal and pleural carcinomatosis produces bloody exudates and cachexia in cirrhotic patients, but repeated cytology revealed reactive mesothelial cells without malignant cells. Clonal hypereosinophilic syndrome was excluded by normal bone marrow morphology and absent immunophenotypic aberrancy on flow cytometry. Autoimmune polyserositis was ruled out by negative ANA, RF, ANCA, and CCP. Strongyloides stercoralis hyperinfection syndrome was confirmed by massive total IgE elevation, positive Strongyloides IgG serology, and complete clinical/radiological cure following ivermectin.
case_prompt:
A 45-year-old man presents to an emergency department in California complaining of progressive abdominal distension and worsening abdominal pain over a 3-week period, accompanied by nonbloody diarrhea and two days of progressive shortness of breath. His past medical history is notable for alcoholic cirrhosis with prior paracentesis, end-stage renal disease on maintenance hemodialysis, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and chronic anemia. He emigrated from Guatemala to the United States four years prior and has a remote history of heavy alcohol use. He denies recent international travel, trauma, fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, hematemesis, or significant weight loss.

On physical examination, he is thin, tachypneic, and in mild respiratory distress. Vital signs reveal a temperature of 97.9°F, blood pressure of 164/93 mm Hg, pulse rate of 87 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 25 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation of 99% on ambient air. Scleral icterus is present. Chest examination demonstrates decreased breath sounds bilaterally at the lung bases. Abdominal examination reveals marked distension with generalized tenderness to palpation without peritoneal signs.

Initial laboratory evaluation demonstrates peripheral blood eosinophilia and an elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase level. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast demonstrates large bilateral pleural effusions with compressive lower lobe atelectasis, splenomegaly, and multiple areas of loculated fluid collections within the peritoneal cavity. Bedside point-of-care ultrasound demonstrates multiple small loculated fluid pockets surrounding the bowel that are unsafe for percutaneous paracentesis, and large bilateral pleural effusions. A diagnostic right-sided thoracentesis yields 500 mL of serosanguinous/bloody fluid; pleural fluid analysis demonstrates an exudative effusion with eosinophilic predominance and elevated red blood cells. Pleural fluid cytology is negative for malignant cells, showing reactive mesothelial cells intermixed with blood elements and prominent eosinophils.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: A bloody, exudative eosinophilic effusion in a cirrhotic patient with loculated ascites raised high concern for serosal malignancy, but repeated cytological examination of pleural fluid and cell blocks demonstrated reactive mesothelial cells without malignant neoplasia.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Cytology of the pleural fluid was negative for malignant cells but showed increased eosinophils intermixed with blood elements and reactive mesothelial cells on cell block material.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Severe peripheral eosinophilia (32%) and serosal infiltration prompted bone marrow biopsy and flow cytometry, which demonstrated reactive eosinophilia with no clonal, myeloid, or lymphoid immunophenotypic aberrancy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: flow cytometry was performed on peripheral blood, revealing 32% eosinophils, but no overt myeloid-associated antigenic aberrancy, myeloblasts, or abnormal subset of T-lymphoid or B-lymphoid cells. Given the patient's persistent eosinophilia, a bone marrow biopsy was performed. Pathology results demonstrated no immunophenotypic abnormality with increased eosinophils likely representing reactive eosinophilia.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Eosinophilic polyserositis can occur in systemic connective tissue diseases or eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, but ANA, RF, ANCA, and anti-CCP autoantibodies were all negative.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: A thorough laboratory work-up was initiated and resulted in negative results for antinuclear antibody (ANA), rheumatoid factor (RF), antineutrophilic cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA), anticyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP) antibodies

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Severe total serum IgE elevation (2549 kU/L) in an immigrant from Guatemala with eosinophilic polyserositis culminated in a positive Strongyloides IgG serology, with rapid normalization of eosinophil count and complete resolution of ascites and effusions following ivermectin therapy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Ultimately, the Strongyloides IgG returned positive, an infectious disease consultation was obtained, and ivermectin was initiated at 200 mcg/kg daily for 2 weeks. Serum eosinophils returned to normal reference laboratory range (<6%) on day 12 of treatment.

editor_comments: Standardized Stanford MedCaseReasoning distillation. Zero pathogen or disease spoilers in case_prompt. Breakpoint set after initial diagnostic thoracentesis. Verbatim quotes verified.
